title: The Second Census: A New Generation Counted
summary: After the plague at Peor, God tells Moses and Eleazar to count Israel again, tribe by tribe and clan by clan, on the plains of Moab. The total comes to 601,730 fighting men, and the land is to be divided among the tribes by size and by lot. The Levites are counted separately, and the chapter closes by noting that not one man counted at Sinai remains except Caleb and Joshua.
story: Numbers opened with a census at Sinai (chapter 1), counting the generation that had come out of Egypt. That generation refused to enter the land at Kadesh (chapters 13 and 14), and God swore that they would die in the wilderness. Nearly forty years later, after a last rebellion and plague at Peor (chapter 25), the sentence has run its course. This second count marks the turn of the book from the old generation to the new. The people are camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, and for the first time the census looks forward to land: these names are the heirs who will receive the inheritance. The chapter also sets up what follows, since the brief mention of Zelophehad's daughters in verse 33 leads directly into their appeal in chapter 27.
historical:
The census takes place in the fortieth year after the exodus, on the eastern side of the Jordan, in territory Israel had just taken from Sihon, king of the Amorites (chapter 21). Eleazar now serves as high priest in place of his father Aaron, who died at Mount Hor (20:22-29). The ancient Near East knew military musters well: kings counted fighting men for war, for labor, and for taxation, and lists of this kind survive from Mesopotamian archives. Israel's count is for war and for the division of land, and it is carried out at God's command rather than a king's.

The numbers themselves raise a well-known question. A total of about six hundred thousand fighting men implies a population of perhaps two million, which is difficult to fit with what is known of the Sinai wilderness and of the population of Canaan in the late Bronze Age. Some scholars, following a line of argument developed by George Mendenhall in the 1950s, suggest that the Hebrew word eleph, usually translated thousand, can also mean a clan unit or military contingent, which would make the figures much smaller. Others take the figures as they stand and point to God's miraculous provision in the wilderness. Still others see the numbers as symbolic or as reflecting a later period. Whatever view one takes, the comparison between the two censuses is the text's point.
cultural:
Israel's society was organized in widening circles: the household (the house of a father), the clan (mishpachah), the tribe, and the whole people. This chapter lists the clans within each tribe, most of them named after the sons and grandsons of Jacob recorded in Genesis 46. Belonging to a clan meant a share in the land, a place in the tribe's fighting force, and a name that would be remembered. Land was not a commodity to be bought and sold at will but an inheritance, held by families and passed down through generations, which is why these lists mattered so much to the first readers.

The method of division combines two principles. Larger tribes receive larger portions (verses 53-54), which is a matter of fairness. But the location of each tribe's territory is decided by lot (verses 55-56), probably using sacred stones or marked objects, which placed the outcome in God's hands and removed it from quarrels and favoritism. Proverbs 16:33 expresses the same conviction: the lot is cast, but its decision is from the LORD.
literary: The chapter is a list with a frame. The frame (verses 1-4 and 63-65) ties the census to Sinai and to the judgment on the old generation. Inside it, each tribe follows the same formula: the descendants of the tribe by their clans, each clan named from its ancestor, and the total. The formula is broken at a few points, and these interruptions are where the meaning is. Verses 9-11 recall Dathan, Abiram, and Korah as a warning sign, adding that Korah's line did not die out. Verse 19 remembers Er and Onan, who died in Canaan. Verse 33 names the five daughters of Zelophehad, and verse 46 names Serah, Asher's daughter. Verses 59-61 trace the family of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam and recall the deaths of Nadab and Abihu. Set side by side with chapter 1, the totals show change: Simeon falls from 59,300 to 22,200, a drop many interpreters connect with the Simeonite leader Zimri at Peor (25:14), while Manasseh grows from 32,200 to 52,700.

The total, and how the land will be divided
None of the old generation remains but Caleb and Joshua

doctrines.note: The closing verses state plainly that God's sentence at Kadesh was carried out: not one of the men counted at Sinai remains. God's warnings are not empty, and unbelief has real consequences.

Even after decades of rebellion and death, Israel is roughly as numerous as before. God preserved the people through the judgment on a generation, and he keeps the line of Korah alive even after Korah's own rebellion.

The census is taken with the land in view. Each clan is counted as an heir of the promise to Abraham, and the division by lot shows that the land is God's gift, not Israel's conquest to share out as it pleases.

words.note: Mishpachah, clan or family. It is the chapter's most frequent word, appearing in nearly every verse of the lists. It names the unit between the household and the tribe, a group of related families descended from a common ancestor. Inheritance in the land was organized by clans, so to be listed here was to have a future in the land.

Nachalah, inheritance. The word describes property passed down within a family and not normally sold outside it. The land is Israel's inheritance because God gives it, and each tribe's share is an inheritance to be kept. The word becomes the key to the last chapters of Numbers, from the appeal of Zelophehad's daughters to the laws of chapter 36.

Goral, lot. The lot was a way of reaching a decision by casting marked objects, understood in Israel not as chance but as a way of receiving God's decision. Its use here means that no tribe could claim it had been cheated by Moses or Joshua; the territories were assigned by the LORD.

christ: The census counts heirs, and the New Testament takes up the language of inheritance for all who belong to Christ. Paul says that those who are Christ's are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:29), and Peter speaks of an inheritance that can never perish, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Hebrews reads the wilderness generation as a warning: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:19). The contrast between a generation that fell and a generation brought to the edge of the promise is a pattern, not a prediction, but it shapes how the New Testament speaks of faith and perseverance. The mention of Joshua at the end is also worth noticing: the one who will lead the people into their inheritance bears the name that, in its Greek form, is Jesus.

hard.q: Can the numbers in Numbers really be right, with over 600,000 fighting men?
hard.a: The figures imply a total population of perhaps two to three million people, which is hard to reconcile with the carrying capacity of the Sinai wilderness and with estimates of Canaan's population at the time. Christians and Jews who hold a high view of Scripture have answered in several ways. One view takes the numbers literally and attributes the people's survival to God's miraculous provision, which the text itself emphasizes (manna, water from the rock). A second view argues that the Hebrew eleph, normally thousand, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that 43,730 might mean 43 units totaling 730 men; this reading faces difficulties with the totals, which add up as thousands in the text as it stands. A third view sees the numbers as deliberately large or symbolic, communicating the fulfillment of God's promise to multiply Abraham's descendants. Others think the figures reflect a later census, such as David's. No solution has won general agreement. What is clear is that the book cares about the comparison: a generation died, and God raised up another of nearly the same size.

questions: The second census is taken after a whole generation has died because of unbelief. What does it mean to you that God keeps his promise to a people even when a generation fails?
The chapter pauses in its lists to remember individuals, including the five daughters of Zelophehad and Serah. Why might it matter that God's record includes names that are easy to overlook?
The land was divided by lot so that no tribe could accuse another of favoritism. Where in your life would it help to receive what you have as a gift rather than something to compare?
